lessons.title: What Is a Search?
body: The Fourth Amendment protects "the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures." Everything in the doctrine depends on a threshold question: did government conduct amount to a "search" or a "seizure" at all? If not, the Amendment is not engaged and no warrant, probable cause, or reasonableness is required.

The Court has given two tests for a search. Under the property-based test, revived in United States v. Jones (2012), a search occurs when the government physically intrudes on a constitutionally protected area (persons, houses, papers, effects) to gather information. Attaching a GPS tracker to a car was such an intrusion. Florida v. Jardines (2013) applied the same idea to a drug-sniffing dog brought onto a home's front porch, which is curtilage, the area immediately surrounding the home. The implied license that lets a visitor walk to the door does not extend to bringing an investigative dog to look for evidence.

Under the privacy-based test from Katz v. United States (1967), a search occurs when the government violates a reasonable expectation of privacy, usually phrased through Justice Harlan's concurrence: the person had an actual, subjective expectation of privacy, and society is prepared to recognize it as reasonable. Katz held that eavesdropping on a phone booth conversation was a search. Kyllo v. United States (2001) held that using a thermal imager to learn about the inside of a home is a search when the technology is not in general public use.

Several categories fall outside the Amendment. Open fields get no protection (Oliver v. United States, 1984), and a person who leaves trash at the curb has no reasonable expectation in it (California v. Greenwood, 1988). Looking at what is exposed to public view, including from lawful airspace (Florida v. Riley, 1989), is not a search. A dog sniff of luggage or of a car during a lawful stop is not a search because it reveals only contraband (Illinois v. Caballes, 2005).

The third-party doctrine says a person has no reasonable expectation in information voluntarily given to a third party, such as bank records (United States v. Miller, 1976) or numbers dialed (Smith v. Maryland, 1979). Carpenter v. United States (2018) declined to extend it mechanically to historical cell-site location information covering seven days or more, holding that acquiring it is a search that generally requires a warrant. The Court called its holding narrow, so lower courts continue to sort out tower dumps, real-time location, and similar data.

Worked example: officers, without a warrant, use a specialized thermal device from the sidewalk to detect the heat pattern of a suspect's living room. Under Kyllo that is a search of the home, and without a warrant or an exception the results are presumptively unreasonable.
Remember the trap: a Fourth Amendment violation requires state action. A private party's search is not covered unless the person is acting as a government agent.

lessons.title: Warrants and Probable Cause
body: The Warrant Clause says that no warrants shall issue "but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized." That yields four requirements: probable cause, an oath or affirmation, particularity, and a neutral and detached magistrate.

Probable cause is a fair probability, not a certainty and not a preponderance. For a search warrant it means a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place. For an arrest warrant it means a fair probability that a particular person committed a crime. Illinois v. Gates (1983) replaced the rigid two-pronged test for informant tips with a totality-of-the-circumstances approach: the informant's veracity and basis of knowledge are still relevant, but a weakness in one can be offset by strength in the other, or by police corroboration of details. Courts review a magistrate's finding with deference, asking only whether there was a substantial basis.

The magistrate must be neutral and detached and capable of determining probable cause. In Coolidge v. New Hampshire (1971), a warrant issued by the state attorney general, who was also leading the investigation, was invalid. The magistrate reads the sworn affidavit and cannot rubber-stamp it.

Particularity prevents general warrants. The warrant must describe the place with enough detail that officers can identify it with reasonable effort, and describe the items sought. A warrant for "evidence of crime" is too broad. In Maryland v. Garrison (1987), officers who reasonably but mistakenly searched the wrong apartment in a building were upheld because the warrant was valid when issued and the mistake was reasonable.

A defendant may challenge the affidavit. Franks v. Delaware (1978) allows a hearing if the defendant makes a substantial preliminary showing that the affiant knowingly or recklessly included a false statement and that the statement was necessary to the finding of probable cause. If at the hearing the defendant proves it, the false material is set aside and the warrant falls if the remainder lacks probable cause. Mere negligence does not qualify.

Execution matters too. Wilson v. Arkansas (1995) held that the common-law knock-and-announce principle is part of reasonableness, though officers may dispense with it on reasonable suspicion of danger or evidence destruction (Richards v. Wisconsin, 1997). Under Hudson v. Michigan (2006), however, violating the rule does not require suppression of the evidence found. Officers executing a search warrant may detain occupants during the search (Michigan v. Summers, 1981).

Worked example: an affidavit states that a reliable informant bought cocaine at a house, and an officer adds a sentence he knows is false to bolster the case. If the defendant shows deliberate falsity at a Franks hearing and the rest of the affidavit does not establish probable cause, the warrant is void and the fruits are subject to suppression.

lessons.title: Arrest, Search Incident, and Vehicles
body: Warrantless searches are presumptively unreasonable, but the Court recognizes a set of narrow exceptions. Three of the most important cluster around arrests and cars.

Arrests first. In a public place, an officer may arrest for a felony on probable cause without a warrant (United States v. Watson, 1976). Entering a home to make a routine arrest is different: Payton v. New York (1980) requires an arrest warrant plus reason to believe the suspect is inside. To arrest a suspect in a third party's home, police need a search warrant for that home (Steagald v. United States, 1981) unless an exception such as consent or exigency applies.

Search incident to arrest allows a search of the arrestee's person and the area within immediate control to find weapons and prevent evidence destruction (Chimel v. California, 1969). A full search of the person incident to a lawful custodial arrest requires no additional justification (United States v. Robinson, 1973). But the rationale limits the scope. Riley v. California (2014) held that police generally may not search the digital contents of a cell phone seized from an arrestee without a warrant, since phones carry vast private information and pose no physical danger. The phone itself may be secured and examined for physical threats.

For vehicles, Arizona v. Gant (2009) narrowed the old rule that allowed searching a car's passenger compartment automatically after any occupant's arrest. Now police may search the passenger compartment incident to arrest only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance, or if it is reasonable to believe the vehicle contains evidence of the offense of arrest. A driver arrested for a traffic offense who is handcuffed in the patrol car generally triggers neither prong.

The automobile exception, from Carroll v. United States (1925), allows a warrantless search of a vehicle based on probable cause that it contains contraband or evidence, because of mobility and a lesser expectation of privacy. The search extends to any container in the car where the object could be found (United States v. Ross, 1982; California v. Acevedo, 1991), including passengers' belongings (Wyoming v. Houghton, 1999). The exception does not allow entering a home's curtilage to search a vehicle parked there (Collins v. Virginia, 2018).

Inventory searches are a separate category: when a car is lawfully impounded, police may inventory its contents under standardized procedures, which are not investigative tools (South Dakota v. Opperman, 1976; Colorado v. Bertine, 1987).

Worked example: police stop Dana for a broken tail light, arrest her on an outstanding fine warrant, cuff her and place her in a squad car, then search the car and find drugs. Under Gant there is no search-incident justification and no reason to believe evidence of the warrant offense is inside. Unless there is independent probable cause, the evidence is suppressible.

lessons.title: Consent, Exigency, and Plain View
body: Consent is the most commonly used exception. A search authorized by voluntary consent needs neither a warrant nor probable cause. Under Schneckloth v. Bustamonte (1973), voluntariness is judged by the totality of the circumstances, and police need not tell the person they may refuse. Factors include age, education, custody, threats or promises, and the number of officers. A false claim of authority, such as "open up, we have a warrant," makes consent invalid because it is acquiescence, not choice.

Who can consent? A person with common authority over the premises can consent as to shared space, and the evidence found can be used against a co-occupant (United States v. Matlock, 1974). Police may also rely on apparent authority if they reasonably, though mistakenly, believe the person had it (Illinois v. Rodriguez, 1990). But when a physically present co-occupant expressly objects, another occupant's consent is ineffective as to that person (Georgia v. Randolph, 2006). If the objector has been lawfully removed, as by a valid arrest, the objection no longer controls (Fernandez v. California, 2014). A consenter may limit scope, and general consent to search a car allows opening containers where the item sought could be found (Florida v. Jimeno, 1991).

Exigent circumstances excuse the warrant requirement when a real emergency leaves no time to get one. Examples include hot pursuit of a fleeing felon (Warden v. Hayden, 1967), preventing imminent destruction of evidence, and rendering emergency aid to someone seriously injured or threatened (Brigham City v. Stuart, 2006). Kentucky v. King (2011) held that police do not create an impermissible exigency by knocking and announcing, as long as they do not violate or threaten to violate the Fourth Amendment. The Court rejected a categorical rule for misdemeanor pursuit (Lange v. California, 2021) and a broad community-caretaking exception for homes (Caniglia v. Strom, 2021). In Missouri v. McNeely (2013), natural dissipation of blood alcohol does not alone create a per se exigency.

Plain view allows seizure of an item if the officer is lawfully in the position from which it is viewed, has lawful access to it, and its incriminating character is immediately apparent, meaning probable cause. Horton v. California (1990) held that the discovery need not be inadvertent. Arizona v. Hicks (1987) shows the limit: moving a stereo to read its serial number was a separate search needing probable cause. Plain feel during a Terry frisk follows the same logic (Minnesota v. Dickerson, 1993).

Worked example: Lee shares a house with Morgan. Police knock, and Lee says Morgan is in the shower and invites them in to look at the shared living room. They see a bag of illegal firearms in plain view. Lee's common authority supports the entry, the lawful vantage point satisfies plain view, and the guns can be seized and used against Morgan, who was not present to object.

lessons.title: Stops, Frisks, and Arrests
body: A seizure of a person occurs when an officer, by physical force or show of authority, restrains liberty. Under United States v. Mendenhall (1980) and Florida v. Bostick (1991), a consensual encounter becomes a seizure when a reasonable person would not feel free to decline the officer's requests or otherwise terminate the encounter. California v. Hodari D. (1991) added that a seizure by show of authority requires actual submission; a fleeing suspect is not seized until caught. Torres v. Madrid (2021) held that the application of physical force with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person escapes.

The Fourth Amendment sorts encounters into tiers. A consensual conversation needs no justification. A brief investigative detention, a Terry stop (Terry v. Ohio, 1968), requires reasonable suspicion, meaning specific and articulable facts that criminal activity is afoot. It is less than probable cause and more than a hunch. A frisk, a pat-down of outer clothing, requires an additional reasonable belief that the person is armed and dangerous, and it is limited to a search for weapons. If the officer feels an object whose contour makes its identity immediately apparent as contraband, it may be seized (Minnesota v. Dickerson, 1993), but squeezing or manipulating it goes too far. An arrest requires probable cause.

Tips and flight are recurring issues. An anonymous tip that lacks predictive detail, such as a bare report that a person is carrying a gun, does not by itself supply reasonable suspicion (Florida v. J.L., 2000), but a 911 call with eyewitness detail and contemporaneous reporting can (Navarette v. California, 2014). Headlong flight upon seeing police, in a high-crime area, may contribute to reasonable suspicion (Illinois v. Wardlow, 2000).

Traffic stops are seizures of the driver and every passenger (Brendlin v. California, 2007). Probable cause or reasonable suspicion of a traffic violation justifies the stop, and the officer's actual motive is irrelevant (Whren v. United States, 1996). Reasonable mistakes of law can still support a stop (Heien v. North Carolina, 2014). Police may order the driver and passengers out of the car (Pennsylvania v. Mimms, 1977; Maryland v. Wilson, 1997) and frisk a passenger with reasonable suspicion of armed danger (Arizona v. Johnson, 2009). The stop may last only as long as needed to handle the mission of the stop; Rodriguez v. United States (2015) held that extending it, even briefly, to conduct a dog sniff without reasonable suspicion is unlawful.

Arrest rules: probable cause suffices for a warrantless custodial arrest even for a minor offense punishable only by a fine (Atwater v. City of Lago Vista, 2001). Moving a suspect to the station for questioning without probable cause is an arrest (Dunaway v. New York, 1979). After a warrantless arrest, a prompt judicial determination of probable cause is required, presumptively within 48 hours (Gerstein v. Pugh, 1975; County of Riverside v. McLaughlin, 1991).

Worked example: an officer sees Jo walking at night near a closed store where a burglary alarm just sounded. Jo ducks into an alley. That alone is thin, but combined with the time, the alarm, and furtive movement it may support reasonable suspicion to stop and ask questions. A frisk would need a further basis to think Jo is armed.

lessons.title: The Exclusionary Rule
body: The exclusionary rule bars the prosecution from using evidence obtained in violation of the Constitution in its case-in-chief. Weeks v. United States (1914) applied it in federal court, and Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied it to the states. The Court today justifies the rule mainly as a deterrent of police misconduct, not as a personal right of the defendant, which is why it is not automatic. The Court has said suppression is a last resort whose costs, releasing possibly guilty people, must be outweighed by deterrence benefits.

The rule reaches derivative evidence, the fruit of the poisonous tree (Wong Sun v. United States, 1963). The question is whether the evidence was obtained by exploitation of the illegality or by means sufficiently distinguishable to purge the taint. Three exceptions limit fruits. Independent source: evidence also obtained through a genuinely separate lawful path is admissible (Murray v. United States, 1988). Inevitable discovery: evidence that would inevitably have been found lawfully is admissible (Nix v. Williams, 1984). Attenuation: the causal chain is broken by intervening events, judged by the factors of Brown v. Illinois (1975), namely time elapsed, intervening circumstances, and the purpose and flagrancy of the misconduct. In Utah v. Strieff (2016), discovery of a valid, preexisting arrest warrant after an unlawful stop attenuated the taint of the stop.

The good-faith exception from United States v. Leon (1984) admits evidence obtained by officers acting in objectively reasonable reliance on a facially valid warrant later found unsupported. It does not apply if the affiant misled the magistrate, the magistrate abandoned the neutral role, the affidavit was so lacking in probable cause that belief in it was unreasonable, or the warrant was facially deficient. Related cases extend good faith to reliance on statutes later struck down (Illinois v. Krull, 1987), court-clerk errors (Arizona v. Evans, 1995), isolated police negligence in recordkeeping (Herring v. United States, 2009), and binding appellate precedent later overruled (Davis v. United States, 2011).

Who may invoke the rule? Fourth Amendment rights are personal, so a defendant must have a legitimate expectation of privacy in the place searched or the item seized (Rakas v. Illinois, 1978). A passenger without a possessory interest usually cannot challenge a car search, though can challenge the stop that detained him. An unauthorized driver of a rental car is not automatically without standing (Byrd v. United States, 2018).

Where the rule does not apply: grand jury proceedings (United States v. Calandra, 1974), civil deportation hearings (INS v. Lopez-Mendoza, 1984), and parole revocation (Pennsylvania Board of Probation and Parole v. Scott, 1998). Illegally seized evidence may impeach a defendant's own testimony (United States v. Havens, 1980). Federal habeas review of Fourth Amendment claims is generally barred if the state provided a full and fair opportunity to litigate (Stone v. Powell, 1976).

Worked example: police unlawfully enter Ray's home and see a ledger, then use what they saw to apply for a warrant. Under Murray, if officers would have sought the warrant anyway on independent information and the unlawful entry did not affect their decision or the magistrate's, the evidence found under the warrant may be admitted.

lessons.title: Miranda v. Arizona
body: The Fifth Amendment says no person "shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself." Miranda v. Arizona (1966) held that the inherently compelling pressures of custodial interrogation require procedural safeguards. Statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible in the prosecution's case-in-chief unless the suspect was warned of the right to remain silent, that anything said can be used in court, the right to consult counsel before and during questioning, and the right to appointed counsel if indigent. Dickerson v. United States (2000) held that Miranda is a constitutional rule that Congress cannot overrule by statute.

Miranda applies only if both custody and interrogation are present. Custody means a formal arrest or restraint of the degree associated with arrest, judged by whether a reasonable person would feel free to terminate the encounter and leave. Ordinary traffic stops are not custody (Berkemer v. McCarty, 1984). The suspect's age is relevant for juveniles (J.D.B. v. North Carolina, 2011). Interrogation means express questioning or its functional equivalent, words or actions police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response (Rhode Island v. Innis, 1980). Volunteered statements are not covered.

Waiver must be knowing, intelligent, and voluntary. It need not be express: Berghuis v. Thompkins (2010) held that a suspect who understood the warnings and then answered questions impliedly waived, and that invoking silence requires an unambiguous statement. Likewise, a request for counsel must be unambiguous, so "maybe I should talk to a lawyer" does not require police to stop (Davis v. United States, 1994). Once a suspect clearly invokes the right to counsel, Edwards v. Arizona (1981) bars further interrogation until counsel is made available or the suspect himself initiates further communication. Maryland v. Shatzer (2010) permits resumed questioning after a 14-day break in custody. Police need not tell a suspect that a lawyer has arrived to speak with him (Moran v. Burbine, 1986).

Exceptions and limits include public safety (New York v. Quarles, 1984), when questions are aimed at an immediate threat, and undercover agents (Illinois v. Perkins, 1990), because a suspect who does not know he is speaking to police feels no coercion. Statements taken in violation of Miranda can still impeach the defendant's testimony if voluntary (Harris v. New York, 1971). Physical fruits of an unwarned but voluntary statement are admissible (United States v. Patane, 2004). A deliberate two-step, questioning first without warnings, then warning and repeating, makes the second statement inadmissible (Missouri v. Seibert, 2004), though a good-faith unwarned slip does not taint a later warned confession (Oregon v. Elstad, 1985). Vega v. Tekoh (2022) held that a Miranda violation does not support a damages action under 42 U.S.C. section 1983.

Worked example: an officer questions Lin at a roadside after a routine stop, then arrests him and continues without warnings. The roadside answers fall outside Miranda for lack of custody, but the post-arrest answers are inadmissible in the case-in-chief and usable only to impeach.

lessons.title: Voluntariness, Massiah, and the Privilege
body: Miranda is not the only constraint on confessions. The Due Process Clauses bar involuntary confessions regardless of warnings. Voluntariness turns on the totality of circumstances, including the suspect's age, intelligence, the length of questioning, and any threats, promises, or physical or psychological pressure. Colorado v. Connelly (1986) held that coercive police activity is a necessary predicate to finding a confession involuntary, so a mentally ill man's confession prompted by internal voices was not excluded. Deception by police is not automatically coercive (Frazier v. Cupp, 1969), though it counts in the totality. A coerced confession is subject to harmless-error analysis (Arizona v. Fulminante, 1991), and an involuntary statement cannot be used even to impeach.

The Sixth Amendment provides a separate protection. The right to counsel attaches at the initiation of adversary judicial proceedings: formal charge, preliminary hearing, indictment, information, or arraignment (Kirby v. Illinois, 1972; Rothgery v. Gillespie County, 2008, holding that attachment occurs at the initial appearance before a magistrate). After attachment, police cannot deliberately elicit statements from the accused outside counsel's presence without a valid waiver (Massiah v. United States, 1964), including through an informant. Brewer v. Williams (1977) applied it to the "Christian burial speech" given to an arraigned suspect in a police car. Unlike Miranda, the Sixth Amendment right is offense-specific (Texas v. Cobb, 2001), covering the charged offense and its legal equivalents under the Blockburger test. Montejo v. Louisiana (2009) allows police to initiate questioning of a represented defendant who has not invoked the right, if the defendant validly waives after Miranda warnings. Massiah applies to deliberate elicitation, so a passive listening informant does not violate it.

The Fifth Amendment privilege itself covers only compelled, testimonial communications. Physical evidence is not testimonial: taking a blood sample (Schmerber v. California, 1966), a voice or handwriting exemplar, fingerprints, or a lineup appearance does not violate it. Whether an act of producing documents is testimonial depends on whether it implicitly communicates existence, possession, or authenticity (Fisher v. United States, 1976; United States v. Hubbell, 2000). The privilege covers any proceeding where an answer might incriminate, but a witness granted use and derivative use immunity can be compelled to testify (Kastigar v. United States, 1972). Statements compelled by threat of job loss cannot be used in a criminal case (Garrity v. New Jersey, 1967). The prosecution may not comment on a defendant's failure to testify at trial (Griffin v. California, 1965), and on request the jury must be told not to draw an adverse inference. Corporations and collective entities have no privilege.

Worked example: Terry is indicted for robbery and released. A police informant, wearing a wire, asks about the robbery, and Terry talks. The statements violate Massiah if the informant deliberately elicited them about the charged offense, even though Terry was not in custody and Miranda did not apply.

lessons.title: Double Jeopardy
body: The Double Jeopardy Clause says no person shall "be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb." Incorporated against the states in Benton v. Maryland (1969), it protects against a second prosecution after acquittal, a second prosecution after conviction, and multiple punishments for the same offense in one proceeding. Its heart is finality: the government, with its resources, should not get repeated attempts to convict.

Attachment. Jeopardy attaches in a jury trial when the jury is empaneled and sworn (Crist v. Bretz, 1978), and in a bench trial when the first witness is sworn. A dismissal before attachment does not bar a new prosecution.

Same offense. Under Blockburger v. United States (1932), two offenses are different if each requires proof of an element the other does not. Conversely, a lesser included offense is the same as the greater offense (Brown v. Ohio, 1977), so conviction of one bars prosecution of the other. The Court rejected a broader same-conduct test in United States v. Dixon (1993). The Blockburger test controls successive prosecutions; in a single trial legislatures may authorize cumulative punishment for offenses that overlap, if clearly expressed.

Acquittal is final even if wrong. The government cannot appeal a jury acquittal, and a judge's acquittal on sufficiency grounds is equally final, even if based on a legal error (Evans v. Michigan, 2013). Ashe v. Swenson (1970) held that collateral estoppel is part of the guarantee: if a jury necessarily decided an issue for the defendant, such as identity, the government cannot relitigate that issue in a later trial for a different offense.

Retrial after conviction. A defendant who wins a reversal on appeal because of trial error may be retried (United States v. Ball, 1896). But if the appellate court reverses because the evidence was legally insufficient, retrial is barred, since that is the equivalent of acquittal (Burks v. United States, 1978). A reversal based on the weight of the evidence is different and allows retrial (Tibbs v. Florida, 1982).

Mistrials. A mistrial declared at the defendant's request or with consent generally does not bar retrial. If declared over objection, retrial is allowed only if there was manifest necessity, such as a hung jury (Arizona v. Washington, 1978). If the prosecutor intentionally provokes a defense mistrial to avoid an acquittal, retrial is barred (Oregon v. Kennedy, 1982).

Separate sovereigns. Two governments with independent sources of authority may each prosecute for the same conduct. Gamble v. United States (2019) reaffirmed the dual-sovereignty doctrine for state and federal prosecutions, and Puerto Rico and tribal cases turn on the source of authority. Many states by statute or constitution restrict successive prosecutions. The Clause covers criminal punishment only; civil penalties generally do not trigger it unless so punitive in effect that they are criminal (Hudson v. United States, 1997).

Worked example: the state acquits Ryan of murder, then the federal government charges him with violating the victim's civil rights based on the same killing. Because the sovereigns are separate, the Clause does not bar the federal case, although Ashe may block relitigating an issue if the identical sovereign were involved.

lessons.title: Charging, Initial Appearance, and Bail
body: The usual path begins with a complaint or arrest, then an initial appearance before a magistrate. There the defendant is informed of the charges and rights, counsel is appointed if needed, and bail is considered. If arrested without a warrant, the defendant is entitled to a prompt judicial determination of probable cause, generally within 48 hours (Gerstein v. Pugh, 1975; County of Riverside v. McLaughlin, 1991). It may be combined with the initial appearance.

Formal charging comes by indictment or information. The Fifth Amendment guarantees a grand jury indictment for federal capital or "otherwise infamous" crimes, but that guarantee is not incorporated against the states (Hurtado v. California, 1884), so many states use a prosecutor's information after a preliminary hearing instead. The grand jury, which in federal court has 16 to 23 members, meets in secret, receives evidence from the prosecutor, and decides whether there is probable cause. The defendant has no right to appear, to have counsel in the room, or to present evidence. The exclusionary rule does not apply (Calandra), hearsay is allowed (Costello v. United States, 1956), and the prosecutor has no constitutional duty to present exculpatory evidence (United States v. Williams, 1992). A grand jury subpoena may be challenged if unreasonable, and a witness may invoke the Fifth Amendment. Discrimination in selection of grand jurors by race requires reversal of a conviction (Vasquez v. Hillery, 1986).

A preliminary hearing, where used (Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 5.1), tests probable cause before a magistrate with counsel, cross-examination, and hearsay generally allowed in many jurisdictions. A later indictment generally moots it. Arraignment follows: the defendant hears the charges and enters a plea. Pretrial motions to dismiss, suppress, or sever are then heard.

Bail. The Eighth Amendment says "excessive bail shall not be required." It does not guarantee a right to bail. Stack v. Boyle (1951) held that bail set higher than is reasonably calculated to assure the defendant's appearance is excessive. United States v. Salerno (1987) upheld the Bail Reform Act of 1984, which permits pretrial detention of a defendant charged with serious crimes upon clear and convincing evidence that no conditions of release can reasonably assure community safety or appearance, after an adversarial hearing. Detention based on dangerousness is regulatory, not punishment. Federal law (18 U.S.C. section 3142) sets a preference for release on the least restrictive conditions and a rebuttable presumption of detention for certain drug and firearm offenses. Cash bail, risk assessment tools, and release without money have been reformed in many states, and approaches vary widely. Debate centers on public safety, the presumption of innocence, and the effect of money-based detention on poor defendants.

Worked example: police arrest Kira without a warrant on Friday night and hold her until Tuesday with no judicial review of probable cause. A 48-hour presumption makes the delay presumptively unreasonable, and the state must show a bona fide emergency or extraordinary circumstance.

lessons.title: Discovery and the Brady Obligation
body: Criminal discovery is narrower than civil discovery. There is no general constitutional right to discovery (Weatherford v. Bursey, 1977). Instead, obligations come from the Due Process Clause, rules, and statutes.

Brady v. Maryland (1963) holds that the prosecution's suppression of evidence favorable to an accused, upon request, violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of good or bad faith. The Court later held that the duty exists with or without a request. Giglio v. United States (1972) extends it to impeachment evidence, such as a deal with a cooperating witness. A Brady violation has three parts (Strickler v. Greene, 1999): the evidence is favorable, either exculpatory or impeaching; it was suppressed by the state, willfully or inadvertently; and prejudice ensued, which means it was material.

Materiality is evaluated collectively. Evidence is material if there is a reasonable probability that, had it been disclosed, the result would have been different, which is less than a preponderance but enough to undermine confidence in the verdict (United States v. Bagley, 1985; Kyles v. Whitley, 1995). Kyles also held that the prosecutor has a duty to learn of favorable evidence known to others acting on the government's behalf, including police. Because materiality can be assessed only after the trial, the duty is often framed as one of disclosure, and prosecutors are expected to err toward disclosure. Many jurisdictions have adopted broader ethics and statutory rules than the constitutional minimum. The prosecution has no constitutional duty to disclose impeachment material before a guilty plea (United States v. Ruiz, 2002).

Beyond Brady: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 16 requires disclosure on request of the defendant's statements, prior record, documents and objects, and reports of examinations and tests, with reciprocal obligations on the defense. The Jencks Act (18 U.S.C. section 3500) requires production of a government witness's prior statements after the witness testifies. Reciprocal discovery from the defendant is limited by the Fifth Amendment but valid where it is fair (Wardius v. Oregon, 1973, requires reciprocity when notice of alibi is demanded). Failure to preserve evidence violates due process only if the police acted in bad faith as to potentially useful evidence (Arizona v. Youngblood, 1988).

Remedies include a new trial, a continuance, or dismissal in rare cases. Prosecutors enjoy absolute immunity from civil suits for trial advocacy conduct (Imbler v. Pachtman, 1976), and the Court has held that a district attorney's office is not liable for a single Brady violation absent a pattern (Connick v. Thompson, 2011), leaving professional discipline as a principal check.

Worked example: a state's key witness testified that he received no benefit for his testimony, but the prosecutor had promised in writing to dismiss his pending charge. After conviction the defense learns of it. The promise is Giglio material, and if there is a reasonable probability that the jury, knowing it, would have returned a different verdict, the conviction must be overturned.

lessons.title: Plea Bargaining
body: Most criminal convictions in the United States, by widely cited estimates well over 90 percent in both federal and state courts, result from guilty pleas rather than trials. The Court has accepted plea bargaining as legitimate because it benefits the defendant, the prosecutor, and the court, while insisting on constitutional limits.

A guilty plea waives several constitutional rights: the privilege against self-incrimination, the right to a jury trial, and the right to confront witnesses (Boykin v. Alabama, 1969). The record must show that the plea is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary. Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11 requires the judge to personally address the defendant, confirm understanding of the charge, rights waived, and maximum and minimum penalties, and find a factual basis. A court may accept a plea even if the defendant maintains innocence where there is strong evidence of guilt (North Carolina v. Alford, 1970), and a nolo contendere plea admits no guilt in later civil actions. Under Rule 11, judges may not participate in plea negotiations.

Prosecutorial leverage is permitted. A prosecutor may offer a lesser charge or sentence recommendation in exchange for a plea (Brady v. United States, 1970). In Bordenkircher v. Hayes (1978), a prosecutor who warned a defendant that he would seek a habitual-offender indictment carrying life if the defendant refused a plea offer did not violate due process, because the threatened charge was supported by probable cause and the defendant was free to accept or reject. A vindictive increase in charges merely for exercising a right after a trial is different. Promises made as part of a plea must be honored: when a prosecutor breaks a promise, the defendant may be entitled to specific performance or withdrawal of the plea (Santobello v. New York, 1971).

Effective assistance applies. Counsel must advise accurately about direct consequences and, under Padilla v. Kentucky (2010), about clear deportation risks. Missouri v. Frye (2012) held that counsel must communicate formal plea offers, and Lafler v. Cooper (2012) held that bad advice causing rejection of a favorable plea can be prejudice, measured by a reasonable probability that the offer would have been accepted, accepted by the court, and led to a lesser sentence. The standard for challenging a plea is a reasonable probability that, but for counsel's error, the defendant would have gone to trial (Hill v. Lockhart, 1985; Lee v. United States, 2017). There is no right to a plea offer, and a defendant has no constitutional right to plead guilty to a particular charge.

Limits on use of pleas. Statements in plea discussions and withdrawn pleas are generally inadmissible (Federal Rule of Evidence 410 and Rule 11(f)), but defendants may waive that protection (United States v. Mezzanatto, 1995). Appeal waivers are common and generally enforceable. A guilty plea normally waives claims of pre-plea constitutional defects, but not a challenge to the government's power to prosecute at all, such as a claim that the statute is unconstitutional (Class v. United States, 2018).

Worked example: defense counsel fails to tell Mara about a prosecutor's formal offer of two years, and she later is convicted at trial and sentenced to six. Under Frye and Lafler, she can show deficient performance, and prejudice if she shows a reasonable probability she would have taken the deal, the court would have approved it, and the sentence would have been lower.

lessons.title: The Right to Counsel
body: The Sixth Amendment guarantees that "in all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall enjoy the right ... to have the Assistance of Counsel for his defence." Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) held that states must appoint counsel for indigent defendants charged with felonies, overruling Betts v. Brady. Argersinger v. Hamlin (1972) and Scott v. Illinois (1979) extended the right to any case in which actual imprisonment is imposed, so a defendant fined only has no right to appointed counsel. Alabama v. Shelton (2002) added that a suspended sentence that could later trigger imprisonment requires counsel.

The right attaches when adversary judicial proceedings begin (Rothgery v. Gillespie County, 2008) and applies at every critical stage, meaning a stage where the defendant's rights may be lost or prejudiced: arraignment (Hamilton v. Alabama, 1961), a preliminary hearing (Coleman v. Alabama, 1970), post-indictment lineups (United States v. Wade, 1967), plea negotiations, trial, and sentencing. It does not apply to pre-charge lineups (Kirby v. Illinois, 1972). On a first appeal as of right, due process and equal protection require counsel (Douglas v. California, 1963), but not for discretionary review (Ross v. Moffitt, 1974) or collateral attack (Pennsylvania v. Finley, 1987).

A defendant may choose to represent himself if the waiver is knowing and voluntary (Faretta v. California, 1975), but a court may appoint standby counsel over objection (McKaskle v. Wiggins, 1984) and may insist on counsel for a defendant competent to stand trial but too impaired to conduct a defense (Indiana v. Edwards, 2008). The right to counsel of choice, for a defendant with the means, is protected, and its erroneous denial is structural error (United States v. Gonzalez-Lopez, 2006), but there is no right to a particular appointed lawyer, and courts may disqualify counsel for serious conflicts (Wheat v. United States, 1988). The privacy of the attorney-client relationship also matters. In McCoy v. Louisiana (2018), counsel may not concede guilt over the client's clear objection, because choosing the objective of the defense belongs to the client.

Ineffective assistance. Strickland v. Washington (1984) requires a defendant to show (1) deficient performance, falling below an objective standard of reasonableness measured by prevailing professional norms, with a strong presumption that conduct was reasonable strategy, and (2) prejudice, a reasonable probability that, but for the error, the result would have been different. Both prongs are required, and a court may resolve the claim on prejudice alone. Prejudice is presumed in narrow situations: complete denial of counsel at a critical stage, counsel who entirely fails to test the prosecution's case (United States v. Cronic, 1984), or an actual conflict of interest that adversely affects performance (Cuyler v. Sullivan, 1980). Examples of deficient performance include failing to conduct any investigation of mitigating evidence (Wiggins v. Smith, 2003), and failing to file a requested appeal (Roe v. Flores-Ortega, 2000). Claims are often raised on collateral review because the trial record may not show counsel's reasons, and federal habeas review of them is doubly deferential.

Worked example: a lawyer in a capital case does not look at the client's records of childhood abuse, and the sentencing jury never hears any mitigating evidence. Under Strickland and Wiggins, the failure to investigate is not a reasoned strategic choice, and if there is a reasonable probability that at least one juror would have voted for a life sentence, relief is warranted.

lessons.title: Confrontation
body: The Confrontation Clause gives the accused the right "to be confronted with the witnesses against him." It guarantees face-to-face meeting at trial, an oath, observation of demeanor, and above all cross-examination. The Clause applies to the states (Pointer v. Texas, 1965).

For decades, Ohio v. Roberts (1980) allowed hearsay if it bore adequate "indicia of reliability." Crawford v. Washington (2004) rejected that approach as unprincipled. Under Crawford, testimonial hearsay offered against a defendant is inadmissible unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. There, a wife's recorded statement to police describing the stabbing, implicating her husband, was testimonial and could not be admitted merely because a court thought it reliable. Reliability is no longer the test. Nontestimonial hearsay is regulated only by evidence law, not by the Clause (Davis v. Washington, 2006).

What is testimonial? Davis drew the line by primary purpose: statements to police in response to interrogation are nontestimonial when the primary purpose is to enable police to meet an ongoing emergency, and testimonial when the primary purpose is to establish past events relevant to later prosecution. Michigan v. Bryant (2011) applied it to a dying victim's statements about the shooter and found them nontestimonial. Ohio v. Clark (2015) held that a young child's statements to a teacher, in the course of detecting abuse, were not testimonial. Statements to friends, casual remarks, and business records are typically nontestimonial, while affidavits, custodial confessions, prior testimony, and formal statements to police are paradigms of testimonial statements.

Forensic reports. Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts (2009) held that sworn certificates of analysis identifying a substance as cocaine are testimonial, so the analyst must be available for cross-examination. Bullcoming v. New Mexico (2011) held that a surrogate analyst who did not conduct or observe the test cannot substitute for the author of a certified report. Williams v. Illinois (2012) produced no majority rationale, and in Smith v. Arizona (2024) the Court held that when an expert conveys an absent analyst's statements as the basis for the expert's opinion, and those statements are offered for their truth, the Clause applies, and the state may not avoid it by labeling them mere "basis" evidence.

Exceptions. A defendant who wrongfully procures a witness's unavailability forfeits confrontation (Giles v. California, 2008, requiring intent to prevent testimony, so a murder defendant's killing of the victim alone is not enough). A child witness may testify by one-way closed-circuit television upon a case-specific finding of necessity (Maryland v. Craig, 1990), though Coy v. Iowa (1988) invalidated a blanket screen rule. Cross-examination about bias is constitutionally protected (Davis v. Alaska, 1974), though judges may limit repetitious inquiry. In joint trials, a nontestifying codefendant's confession that expressly names the defendant cannot be admitted at the joint trial even with a limiting instruction (Bruton v. United States, 1968), but redacted confessions that do not obviously point to the defendant are permitted (Richardson v. Marsh, 1987). If the declarant testifies at trial and is subject to cross-examination, the Clause does not bar the prior statements.

Worked example: police arrive at a home after a call. A woman, now calm and in the kitchen, describes how her boyfriend hit her an hour earlier, and she signs an affidavit. She does not testify at trial. The primary purpose of the exchange was to establish past events, so the statements are testimonial and, absent prior cross-examination or forfeiture, inadmissible against him.

lessons.title: Jury Trial and Speedy Trial
body: The jury right. The Sixth Amendment guarantees an impartial jury in criminal prosecutions, and Duncan v. Louisiana (1968) applied it to the states for serious offenses. Petty offenses, those with a maximum authorized penalty of six months or less, carry no jury right (Baldwin v. New York, 1970; Blanton v. City of North Las Vegas, 1989), unless additional statutory penalties make them serious.

Jury size and unanimity. Twelve is not constitutionally required. Williams v. Florida (1970) upheld six-person juries, but Ballew v. Georgia (1978) held five too few. Burch v. Louisiana (1979) required unanimity for six-person juries. For twelve-person juries, Apodaca v. Oregon (1972) tolerated nonunanimous verdicts, but Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) overruled it and held that the Sixth Amendment, as incorporated, requires a unanimous verdict to convict of a serious offense in state court. In Edwards v. Vannoy (2021) the Court held Ramos does not apply retroactively on federal collateral review.

The jury venire and selection. The jury pool must be drawn from a fair cross-section of the community (Taylor v. Louisiana, 1975; Duren v. Missouri, 1979), but the petit jury itself need not mirror the community. During voir dire, jurors may be removed for cause for bias, and each side has peremptory challenges. Batson v. Kentucky (1986) forbids peremptory strikes based on race, using a three-step framework: the opponent makes a prima facie showing of discrimination, the striking party gives a race-neutral explanation, and the court decides whether purposeful discrimination was shown. It was extended to gender (J.E.B. v. Alabama ex rel. T.B., 1994) and applies to the defense (Georgia v. McCollum, 1992). Flowers v. Mississippi (2019) emphasized the importance of context and the history of a prosecutor's strikes. In capital cases, jurors may be excluded for cause only if their views on capital punishment would prevent or substantially impair their duties (Wainwright v. Witt, 1985).

Judge versus jury. The Sixth Amendment requires that any fact increasing the maximum penalty, other than a prior conviction, be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt (Apprendi v. New Jersey, 2000), which applies to state sentencing schemes (Blakely v. Washington, 2004), to the federal guidelines, which became advisory (United States v. Booker, 2005), and to facts triggering mandatory minimums (Alleyne v. United States, 2013). Ring v. Arizona (2002) required that a jury find capital aggravating factors. Erlinger v. United States (2024) applied the principle to the question whether prior offenses were committed on separate occasions for purposes of the Armed Career Criminal Act.

Speedy trial. The Sixth Amendment right attaches at arrest or formal charge (United States v. Marion, 1971). Barker v. Wingo (1972) gave a balancing test with four factors: length of delay, reason for delay, the defendant's assertion of the right, and prejudice. Courts treat delays approaching a year as presumptively prejudicial triggers for analysis, and Doggett v. United States (1992) found a violation after an eight-and-a-half-year delay mostly attributable to government negligence even without specific proof of prejudice. The remedy is dismissal with prejudice (Strunk v. United States, 1973). The right does not apply to sentencing delay (Betterman v. Montana, 2016). The Speedy Trial Act of 1974 sets federal deadlines: an indictment within 30 days of arrest and trial within 70 days of indictment or first appearance, excluding specified periods. Pre-indictment delay is governed by due process and statutes of limitations (United States v. Lovasco, 1977).

Worked example: a prosecutor in a trial of a Black defendant strikes four of five Black venire members, explaining that they are "too young." The record shows she did not strike young white jurors with similar profiles. A court applying Batson may find that the stated reason is pretextual.

lessons.title: The Eighth Amendment
body: The Eighth Amendment provides: "Excessive bail shall not be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted." It is incorporated against the states. Courts interpret "cruel and unusual" in light of the "evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society" (Trop v. Dulles, 1958), assessed with objective indicia such as state legislation and sentencing practice, plus the Court's own judgment.

Methods of punishment. Methods that are barbaric or involve the unnecessary infliction of pain are forbidden. Baze v. Rees (2008) and Glossip v. Gross (2015) upheld lethal injection protocols, and Bucklew v. Precythe (2019) held that a prisoner challenging a method must propose a feasible alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain. The Court has also held that the Amendment bars punishing a status such as addiction (Robinson v. California, 1962), though it did not bar punishing public drunkenness (Powell v. Texas, 1968).

Proportionality in noncapital sentences. The Amendment has a narrow proportionality principle. Solem v. Helm (1983) struck down life without parole for a seventh nonviolent felony, but Harmelin v. Michigan (1991) upheld life without parole for possessing a large quantity of cocaine, and Ewing v. California (2003) and Lockyer v. Andrade (2003) upheld California's three-strikes sentences. The Court looks to the gravity of the offense and harshness of the penalty, and successful challenges are rare.

Capital punishment. This subject is contested, and the law and the debate should be kept separate. As a matter of current law, the death penalty is constitutional: Furman v. Georgia (1972) struck down arbitrary capital sentencing schemes, and Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld guided-discretion schemes with bifurcated trials, aggravating circumstances, and individualized sentencing. Mandatory death sentences are unconstitutional (Woodson v. North Carolina, 1976), and the sentencer must be permitted to consider any mitigating evidence (Lockett v. Ohio, 1978). Categorical exclusions have been recognized: nonhomicide offenses against individuals, including rape of an adult (Coker v. Georgia, 1977) and rape of a child (Kennedy v. Louisiana, 2008); persons with intellectual disability (Atkins v. Virginia, 2002; Hall v. Florida, 2014); offenders under 18 at the time of the offense (Roper v. Simmons, 2005); and those insane at the time of execution (Ford v. Wainwright, 1986). Defendants whose participation in a killing was minor are subject to an individual-culpability requirement (Enmund v. Florida, 1982; Tison v. Arizona, 1987).

Supporters stress retribution for the gravest crimes, the interests of victims' families, and democratic choice. Critics stress the risk of executing innocent people, uneven application by race, geography and quality of counsel, cost, and doubts about deterrence. A majority of states retain capital punishment by statute, but several have abolished it, and the situation changes, so current status should be checked.

Juveniles. Graham v. Florida (2010) bars life without parole for juveniles who did not commit homicide. Miller v. Alabama (2012) bars mandatory life without parole for juvenile homicide offenders, requiring individualized consideration of youth, and Montgomery v. Louisiana (2016) made it retroactive. Jones v. Mississippi (2021) held that a sentencer need not make a separate finding of permanent incorrigibility.

Conditions and fines. Prison officials violate the Amendment through deliberate indifference to serious medical needs (Estelle v. Gamble, 1976) or substantial risks of harm (Farmer v. Brennan, 1994), and Brown v. Plata (2011) upheld a population cap remedy for unconstitutional overcrowding. The Excessive Fines Clause bars fines grossly disproportional to the offense (United States v. Bajakajian, 1998), and was incorporated in Timbs v. Indiana (2019).

Worked example: a state mandates life without parole for any person convicted of murder, including a 16-year-old. Under Miller, a mandatory scheme with no chance to consider youth and attendant circumstances is unconstitutional as applied to the juvenile.

lessons.title: Special Needs, Borders, and Supervised Persons
body: The Fourth Amendment's baseline is a warrant on probable cause. For some searches, the Court uses a general reasonableness balancing that weighs the intrusion on privacy against the government interest, and it sometimes dispenses with individualized suspicion. The key divider is purpose: searches serving ordinary crime control generally need individualized suspicion, while those serving "special needs" beyond normal law enforcement may not.

Administrative searches. Camara v. Municipal Court (1967) required warrants for housing inspections, but allowed them on a showing of reasonable legislative or administrative standards rather than probable cause of a violation. Closely regulated industries, such as liquor or firearms dealers and mines, may be inspected without warrants under a statute that is a constitutionally adequate substitute.

Schools and workplaces. In New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985), school officials may search a student on reasonable suspicion rather than probable cause, if the search is reasonably related to the objective and not excessively intrusive. Safford Unified School District v. Redding (2009) held that a strip search for ibuprofen was unreasonable. Suspicionless drug testing is allowed for student athletes (Vernonia School District v. Acton, 1995) and for students in competitive extracurricular activities (Board of Education v. Earls, 2002), and for certain railway employees and customs officers in safety-sensitive jobs (Skinner v. Railway Labor Executives' Association, 1989; National Treasury Employees Union v. Von Raab, 1989). But the Court struck down testing of candidates for state office (Chandler v. Miller, 1997) and a hospital program that shared drug-test results with police (Ferguson v. City of Charleston, 2001) because its primary purpose was law enforcement.

Checkpoints. Fixed sobriety checkpoints are valid (Michigan Department of State Police v. Sitz, 1990), as are fixed immigration checkpoints near the border (United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, 1976). A roadblock whose primary purpose is general crime control, such as drug interdiction, is not (Indianapolis v. Edmond, 2000). An information-seeking checkpoint about a recent crime can be reasonable (Illinois v. Lidster, 2004).

Borders. Routine searches of persons and property at the border or its functional equivalent need no warrant or suspicion (United States v. Ramsey, 1977; United States v. Flores-Montano, 2004, upholding disassembly of a gas tank). Highly intrusive searches of the person, such as a body cavity search, require reasonable suspicion. Forensic searches of electronic devices at the border have divided the lower courts on what suspicion is required, and the Supreme Court has not resolved it.

Probation, parole, and arrestees. Probationers may be searched on reasonable suspicion when a condition of probation authorizes it (United States v. Knights, 2001). Parolees, who have a lesser expectation of privacy, may be searched without any suspicion (Samson v. California, 2006). Taking a DNA swab from persons arrested for serious offenses and brought to custody is a reasonable booking procedure (Maryland v. King, 2013).

Worked example: a high school vice principal receives a report that Ty was seen with a vape cartridge and searches his backpack. Under T.L.O. the search is reasonable at its inception if there are reasonable grounds to suspect a rule violation, and reasonable in scope if it matches the suspected violation. Searching his underwear for a cartridge would require much more.

lessons.title: Due Process at Trial
body: In re Winship (1970) held that due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the charged crime. The presumption of innocence is a central principle, and the court must instruct the jury on it on request in appropriate cases (Taylor v. Kentucky, 1978). The state may not shift the burden on an element through a mandatory presumption (Sandstrom v. Montana, 1979), but may place the burden on the defendant to prove an affirmative defense that does not negate an element (Patterson v. New York, 1977), so the allocation depends on how the legislature defines the offense.

Sufficiency. A conviction violates due process if no rational trier of fact could have found guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution (Jackson v. Virginia, 1979). A trial judge may enter a judgment of acquittal under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 29, which, once granted, is final.

Competence and presence. A defendant must be competent to stand trial, meaning he has sufficient present ability to consult with counsel with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings (Dusky v. United States, 1960). A state may not require the defendant to prove incompetence by clear and convincing evidence (Cooper v. Oklahoma, 1996). A defendant has a right to be present, but may forfeit it by disruptive conduct (Illinois v. Allen, 1970). Visible shackles are not allowed in front of a jury without case-specific justification (Deck v. Missouri, 2005), nor may the defendant be compelled to wear prison clothes (Estelle v. Williams, 1976).

Public trial and fairness. The Sixth Amendment guarantees a public trial, and closing a courtroom requires an overriding interest, narrowly tailored closure, and findings (Waller v. Georgia, 1984; Presley v. Georgia, 2010). Pervasive pretrial publicity can warrant change of venue, but the question is whether jurors can be impartial (Irvin v. Dowd, 1961; Skilling v. United States, 2010).

Defense rights. The defendant has a constitutional right to testify (Rock v. Arkansas, 1987), compulsory process to obtain witnesses (Washington v. Texas, 1967), and a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense (Chambers v. Mississippi, 1973; Holmes v. South Carolina, 2006), though evidence rules that serve legitimate purposes are not invalid merely because they exclude defense evidence. The prosecution violates due process by knowingly using false testimony or failing to correct it (Napue v. Illinois, 1959).

Eyewitness identification. Due process bars admission of an identification produced by an unnecessarily suggestive police procedure only if, under the totality, the identification is not reliable, considering opportunity to view, attention, accuracy of the description, certainty, and time elapsed (Neil v. Biggers, 1972; Manson v. Brathwaite, 1977). Perry v. New Hampshire (2012) held that this inquiry applies only when police arranged the suggestive circumstances. Many jurisdictions give cautionary instructions on eyewitness reliability.

Harmless error. Most constitutional errors are subject to harmless-error review, requiring the state to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the error did not contribute to the verdict (Chapman v. California, 1967). A small class of structural errors defeats the framework and requires automatic reversal, including complete denial of counsel, denial of counsel of choice, a biased judge, denial of a public trial, a defective reasonable-doubt instruction, and denial of self-representation. Some structural claims, when raised on direct review through a claim of ineffective assistance, still require a showing of prejudice (Weaver v. Massachusetts, 2017). Plain error review applies to unpreserved claims on appeal (Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 52(b); United States v. Olano, 1993).

Worked example: an officer, in a showup shortly after a robbery, tells the victim, "We caught the guy, is this him?" The identification procedure was suggestive, but under Biggers and Brathwaite it is admissible if the victim had a good view in good light, gave a detailed prior description, and was certain.

lessons.title: Appeals, Preservation, and Finality
body: There is no federal constitutional right to appeal a criminal conviction, but every state and the federal system provide one, and once provided it must be administered consistent with due process and equal protection. Griffin v. Illinois (1956) held that a state may not deny an indigent a transcript needed for appeal. Douglas v. California (1963) requires counsel on a first appeal as of right. When appointed counsel concludes that an appeal is frivolous, counsel must file a brief referring to anything in the record that arguably supports the appeal and request leave to withdraw, and the court then reviews the record (Anders v. California, 1967).

Mechanics. In federal court, a defendant ordinarily must file a notice of appeal within 14 days after entry of judgment (Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(b)). State deadlines vary. The prosecution generally cannot appeal an acquittal but may appeal some pretrial rulings such as suppression orders (18 U.S.C. section 3731). Interlocutory appeals are limited, and the final-judgment rule normally means the defendant waits until sentencing, with narrow exceptions such as denials of double jeopardy motions.

Preservation. To obtain review, a party generally must make a timely, specific objection at trial and obtain a ruling. A motion to suppress must be made before trial (Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 12). A failure to object forfeits the issue, and review then lies only for plain error: an error, that is plain or clear, that affects substantial rights, and that seriously affects the fairness, integrity, or public reputation of judicial proceedings (United States v. Olano, 1993). Waiver, the intentional relinquishment of a known right, bars review entirely. Appellate courts defer to trial findings of fact, applying clear error review, and review questions of law de novo. Evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

Standards of reversal. A preserved constitutional error triggers Chapman's harmless-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard, with the state bearing the burden. Nonconstitutional errors are harmless if they did not have a substantial influence on the outcome (Kotteakos v. United States, 1946). Insufficient evidence leads to acquittal, while trial error leads to a new trial. Appeal waivers contained in plea agreements are generally enforceable.

Finality. Once direct review ends, either because the time to seek certiorari expires or the Court denies it, the judgment is final. Finality supports the retroactivity rules in habeas (Teague v. Lane, 1989) and the one-year habeas limitations period. The pressure of finality creates the tension between correcting error and preserving closure that the next lesson addresses. Collateral attack, such as a state postconviction petition, can raise claims that could not be raised earlier, such as ineffective assistance or newly discovered evidence, and most states have their own time limits and procedural bars. Executive clemency and pardons are a separate, discretionary path.

Worked example: a defendant who did not object when the prosecutor commented on his silence at trial raises the point for the first time on appeal. Review is for plain error. Griffin v. California makes the comment error, and it is plain, but the defendant must also show that it affected his substantial rights, usually by showing a reasonable probability of a different result.

lessons.title: Habeas Corpus
body: Habeas corpus, "you have the body," is the writ by which a court tests the lawfulness of detention. The Constitution protects it in the Suspension Clause (Article I, section 9), and Boumediene v. Bush (2008) applied it to detainees held at Guantanamo Bay. In criminal practice the main vehicles are 28 U.S.C. section 2254, which lets federal courts review the custody of state prisoners, and section 2255, which lets federal prisoners attack their sentence in the sentencing court. The petitioner must be "in custody," which includes parole and probation, and must allege a violation of federal law.

AEDPA. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 sharply restricted habeas. It sets a one-year limitation period, running generally from the date the judgment becomes final, tolled during pending state postconviction review. It limits second or successive petitions and requires a certificate of appealability. Most important, section 2254(d) bars relief on any claim adjudicated on the merits in state court unless the state decision was contrary to, or an unreasonable application of, clearly established federal law as determined by the Supreme Court, or was based on an unreasonable determination of the facts (Williams v. Taylor, 2000). Only Supreme Court holdings, not lower-court decisions, count as clearly established law. "Unreasonable" means more than incorrect: Harrington v. Richter (2011) held that relief is available only where there is no possibility fairminded jurists could disagree that the state court's decision conflicts with Supreme Court precedent, and that the standard applies even to a summary denial without opinion. Review of the facts is limited to the record before the state court (Cullen v. Pinholster, 2011).

Exhaustion and procedural default. A petitioner must first present claims to the state courts (28 U.S.C. section 2254(b); Rose v. Lundy, 1982). If a claim was not properly presented and state remedies are now barred, it is procedurally defaulted, and a federal court may reach it only upon showing cause and prejudice (Wainwright v. Sykes, 1977; Coleman v. Thompson, 1991) or a fundamental miscarriage of justice, meaning a credible showing of actual innocence (Schlup v. Delo, 1995; McQuiggin v. Perkins, 2013). Martinez v. Ryan (2012) created a narrow equitable exception for defaults caused by ineffective postconviction counsel on trial-ineffectiveness claims, which Shinn v. Ramirez (2022) sharply limited by restricting new evidence.

Other limits. Fourth Amendment exclusionary claims are not cognizable if the state gave a full and fair chance to litigate them (Stone v. Powell, 1976). New rules of criminal procedure generally do not apply retroactively to final convictions (Teague v. Lane, 1989), except for substantive rules and, in theory, watershed rules of fundamental fairness, a category the Court has said is effectively empty (Edwards v. Vannoy, 2021). On trial-type errors, the petitioner must show a substantial and injurious effect on the verdict (Brecht v. Abrahamson, 1993). A freestanding claim of actual innocence has not been recognized by the Court as a basis for relief in a noncapital case (Herrera v. Collins, 1993, assuming without deciding for a capital case).

Contested policy. Proponents of AEDPA's limits stress finality, federalism, respect for state courts, and the burden on victims of repeated litigation. Critics stress that federal courts are an important check on constitutional violations and wrongful convictions, and that procedural rules sometimes block meritorious claims.

Worked example: a state prisoner whose conviction became final in January files a federal petition 18 months later alleging that his lawyer failed to investigate. No state petition was pending. The petition is likely time-barred under the one-year period unless equitable tolling or a statutory exception applies, and the court would not reach the merits.

questions.prompt: Which test did United States v. Jones (2012) rely on when it held that attaching a GPS device to a car was a search?
choices: A reasonable expectation of privacy in the car's public movements over a short trip
A balancing of the intrusion against the government's need for the information
A requirement that the technology used was not in general public use
A physical intrusion on a protected effect for the purpose of obtaining information

questions.prompt: Officers bring a trained drug-detection dog onto the enclosed front porch of a suspect's house and the dog alerts at the door. Under the Court's case law, this is most likely:
choices: Not a search, because the porch is visible from the street and any visitor may walk up and knock
A search only if the handler lacked reasonable suspicion that drugs were inside before bringing the dog up
A search, because the porch is curtilage and the implied license to approach does not cover this
Not a search, because a dog sniff reveals only contraband, so no legitimate privacy interest is invaded

questions.prompt: What did Carpenter v. United States (2018) decide?
choices: Cell-site records are protected only if the user took affirmative steps to disable location services before the data was generated
Acquiring seven or more days of historical cell-site location records is generally a search requiring a warrant
The third-party doctrine was abolished, so no business record is ever available to police without a warrant
Real-time tracking of a phone is always a search, but historical location records held by carriers never are

questions.prompt: Without a warrant, an officer stands on a public sidewalk and aims a specialized thermal imager, not available to the general public, at Rowan's house. It reveals heat patterns suggesting grow lamps inside. Rowan moves to suppress the results. The most likely ruling is that the motion is:
choices: Granted, because using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to learn about the home's interior is a search
Denied, because the officer stood on a public sidewalk and observed only heat that radiated off the exterior of the house
Denied, because heat waste emitted from a house is voluntarily exposed to the public in the same way as trash left at the curb
Granted, but only if the imager revealed intimate details of the home such as the people present or their private activities

questions.prompt: A bank teller, acting entirely on her own after noticing suspicious activity, copies a customer's private letters from a safe-deposit box and mails them to the police. The police read them without a warrant. The customer moves to suppress. The most likely outcome is that the motion is:
choices: Granted, because the contents of sealed letters carry a reasonable expectation of privacy against all intrusions
Granted, because police acquisition of private papers requires a warrant even when a private party supplied them
Denied, because the third-party doctrine strips protection from anything stored at a bank
Denied, because the teller's private search is not state action and the police may examine what she revealed

questions.prompt: What standard of proof does probable cause represent for a search warrant?
choices: A fair probability that contraband or evidence will be found in the place to be searched
A preponderance of the evidence that the suspect committed the crime under investigation
Clear and convincing evidence that the items sought are inside the place to be searched
Proof beyond a reasonable doubt that a crime occurred and that evidence is on the premises

questions.prompt: A defendant claims that the affidavit for a search warrant contained a false statement. To obtain a Franks hearing the defendant must make a substantial preliminary showing that:

The seizure is valid because the stereo was in plain view and the officers were lawfully present in the home

The Clause applies only when the absent analyst's statements appear in a signed and sworn affidavit or certificate

Imposing life without parole for a third serious felony committed by an adult

Only the most disputed element beyond a reasonable doubt
